Balancing Weights, Directed Sparsification, and Augmenting Paths

**Abstract**

We present a randomized augmenting paths-based algorithm to compute the maximum flow in a directed, uncapacitated graph in almost _m+nF_ time, matching the algorithm of Karger and Levine for undirected graphs (SICOMP 2015). Combined with an initial \(\sqrt{n}\) rounds of blocking flow to reduce the value of _F_, we obtain a maximum flow algorithm with running time _mn_<sup>1/2+_o_(1)</sup>. For combinatorial, augmenting paths-based algorithms, this is the first improvement over Dinic’s algorithm for moderately sparse graphs.

To obtain our algorithm, we introduce a new technique to re-weight the edges of a strongly connected directed graph so that each cut is approximately balanced: the total weight of edges in one direction is within a constant factor of the total weight in the other direction. We then adapt Karger and Levine’s technique of sampling edges from the newly weighted residual graph, ensuring that an augmenting path exists in the sampled graph with high probability. One technical difficulty is that our balancing weights have to be dynamically maintained upon changes to the residual graph. Surprisingly, we can black box the dynamic data structure from the recent interior point method-based flow algorithm of van den Brand et al. (FOCS 2024).

## 1 Introduction

In the (uncapacitated) maximum flow problem, we are given a directed graph and two vertices _s_ and _t_, and the goal is to find the maximum number of edge-disjoint paths from _s_ to _t_. It is one of the oldest problems in combinatorial optimization [Dan51], and many influential techniques have been developed to tackle the problem, including augmenting paths [FF56], blocking flows [Din70], push-relabel [GT88], and random sampling [KL15]. More recently, techniques based on continuous optimization have become widely successful, culminating in the first almost-linear time algorithm for maximum flow and its generalizations [CKL<sup>+</sup>25]. However, it remains an open question whether a more traditional approach based on augmenting paths can match this recent breakthrough. Two very recent lines of work have obtained almost quadratic-time algorithms for maximum flow [BBST24, BBL<sup>+</sup>25] and bipartite matching [CK24a, CK24b], showing that combinatorial techniques still have room for future development.

In this work, we present a new approach based on sampling edges from an appropriately weighted residual graph. Our main result is the following:

**Theorem 1.** _There is a randomized, augmenting paths-based algorithm that computes the maximum flow on a directed, uncapacitated graph in time_ \((m+nF)\cdot n^{o(1)}\)_, where F is the value of the maximum flow._

Combined with an initial \(\sqrt{n}\) rounds of blocking flow to ensure that \(F\le m/\sqrt{n}\), we obtain the following corollary:

**Corollary 2.** _There is a randomized, augmenting paths-based algorithm that computes the maximum flow on a directed, uncapacitated graph in time mn_<sup>1/2+_o_(1)</sup>.

For augmenting paths-based algorithms, this is the first improvement over Dinic’s algorithm \[Din70\] for moderately sparse graphs, which runs in time \(O(m\cdot min\{m^{1/2},n^{2/3}\})\) as analyzed by Karzanov \[Kar73\] and Even and Tarjan \[ET75\].

## 1.1 Our Techniques

Our starting point is Karger and Levine’s algorithm on _undirected_ graphs \[KL15\], which finds each augmenting path in a random sample of the residual graph. At a high level, Karger and Levine show that if the algorithm has sent a \((1-\epsilon)\)-fraction of the maximum flow, then the residual graph is \(O(1/\epsilon)\)-balanced in the following sense: for any cut, viewed as a bipartition (_S,V_\\_S_) of the vertex set, the number of edges going from _S_ to _V_\\_S_ is within a multiplicative \(O(1/\epsilon)\)-factor of the number of edges going from _V_\\_S_ to _S_. Then, they employ the random sampling method of Benczúr and Karger for undirected graphs \[BK15\], accounting for the balance of \(O(1/\epsilon)\) by over- sampling at a rate of \(O(1/\epsilon)\). Overall, they show that sampling \(\tilde{O}(n/\epsilon)^1\) edges is sufficient with high probability<sup>2</sup>, so the next augmenting path can be found in time \(\tilde{O}(n/\epsilon)\). Since most of the augmenting paths are found when \(\epsilon\) is still constant, the amortized running time per augmenting path is \(\tilde{O}(n)\), establishing their running time of \(\tilde{O}(m+nF)\).

Unfortunately, the balance guarantee no longer holds if the input graph is directed. For example, suppose the input graph has an unbalanced cut (_S,V_\\_S_) with \(s\in S\) and \(t\in V\backslash S\), with only a single edge going from _S_ to _V_\\_S_ but many edges in the opposite direction. Since Karger and Levine’s algorithm treats the residual graph as undirected for the purpose of sampling, the single edge from _S_ to _V_\\_S_ cannot be distinguished from the edges in the opposite direction, and is therefore unlikely to be sampled. If the edge is not sampled, then there cannot be a path from _s_ to _t_, invalidating the approach.

Our main idea is to re-weight the residual graph so that any cut is balanced in terms of weight: the total weight of edges in one direction is within a constant factor of the total weight in the other direction. In the example above, the single edge from _S_ to _V_\\_S_ must have much higher weight than the edges in the opposite direction. We then treat the graph as undirected but _weighted_ when sampling edges, so that the single edge from _S_ to _V_\\_S_ is likely to be sampled.

One technical difficulty is that our balancing weights have to be dynamically maintained upon changes to the residual graph. More precisely, when an augmenting path is found, the residual graph is updated by flipping each edge along the path. Since Karger and Levine treat the graph as undirected for the purpose of sampling, flipping an edge does not change their sampling probabilities. However, our balancing weights are sensitive to edge flips, and a dynamic algorithm is required to maintain them. Surprisingly, we show that the _minimum ratio cut_ framework from the recent interior point method-based flow algorithm of van den Brand et al. \[VDBCK<sup>+</sup>24\] can be adapted to compute balancing weights. In particular, we completely black box their data structure for maintaining approximate minimum ratio cuts. We remark that this data structure is purely combinatorial and is comparable in complexity to the data structures in \[CK24a, CK24b\].

<sup>1</sup>\(\tilde{O}(\cdot)\) ignores factors poly-logarithmic in _n_. <sup>2</sup>_With high probability_ means with probability 1-1_/n<sup>c</sup>_ for arbitrarily large constant _c_.

## 1.2 Related Work

The concept of _balance_ for directed graphs is introduced by Ene et al. \[EMPS16\], who show that existing techniques for undirected flow-based problems can be translated to directed graphs that are approximately balanced. For graphs that are _perfectly_ balanced, namely the Eulerian graphs, Cohen et al. \[CKK<sup>+</sup>18\] use directed graph sparsification to obtain fast algorithms for solving directed Laplacian systems. Sparsification for approximately balanced graphs is systematically studied by Cen et al. \[CCPS21\], who obtain tight upper and lower bounds for various types of sparsification. All of these results are restricted to balanced graphs, and to the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to employ techniques from balanced graphs in the context of general directed graphs.

## 1.3 Preliminaries

Throughout the paper, all graphs are uncapacitated, either weighted or unweighted, and either directed or undirected. We refer to directed edges as _arcs_ and undirected edges as _edges_. The input directed graph to maximum flow is assumed to be _G_=(_V,E_), with vertices \(s,t\in V\) . We define a _flow_ from _s_ to _t_ as a set of arc-disjoint paths from _s_ to _t_ in _G_, and the _value_ of the flow is the number of paths in the set. The _residual graph G<sub>f</sub>_ is obtained from _G_ by flipping each arc along each path in _f_. The standard augmenting paths framework attempts to find a path from _s_ to _t_ in _G<sub>f</sub>_, called an _augmenting path_. If a path is found, then each arc along the path is flipped, and the flow _f_ is updated accordingly. Otherwise, if no path exists, then _f_ is a maximum flow, and the algorithm terminates.

A _cut_ is a bipartition (_S,V_\\_S_) of the vertex set into two non-empty subsets, represented as one of the sides \(S\subseteq V\) . The _boundary_ \(\partial S\) of the cut is the set of arcs/edges with exactly one endpoint in _S_. For a directed graph, the out-boundary \(\partial^+S\) is the set of arcs with only the tail in _S_, and the in-boundary \(\partial^-S\) is the set of arcs with only the head in _S_. For a weighted graph with weight function _w_, let \(w(\partial S)\) denote the total weight of arcs/edges in \(\partial S\), and define \(w(\partial^+S)\) and \(w(\partial^-S)\) similarly. For an unweighted graph, let \(|\partial S|\) denote the number of arcs/edges in \(\partial S\), and define \(|\partial^+S|\) and \(|\partial^-S|\) similarly.

## 1.4 Preprocessing the Graph

We first preprocess the graph as follows. First, add _m_ many parallel arcs (_t,s_), which does not affect the maximum flow from _s_ to _t_. Then, compute the strongly connected components of the new graph. If _s_ and _t_ do not belong to the same strongly connected component, then the existence of arc (_t,s_) implies that there is no path from _s_ to _t_, and the algorithm concludes that the maximum flow from _s_ to _t_ has value 0. Otherwise, discard all strongly connected components except the one containing _s_ and _t_, and solve the maximum flow problem on the remaining component. This operation is safe because there is no path from _s_ to _t_ that contains vertices outside the strongly connected component containing _s_ and _t_.

Let _G_ be the resulting graph after preprocessing. The lemma below ensures that any residual graph _G<sub>f</sub>_ remains strongly connected as long as the current flow is not maximum.

**Lemma 3.** _Let f be a flow from s to t in G that does not use any arc_ (_t,s). If there is a path from s to t in G<sub>f</sub>, then G<sub>f</sub> is strongly connected._

_Proof._ It suffices to show that \(\partial_{G_f}^+S\neq\emptyset\) for any cut \(S\subseteq V\) . By assumption, all arcs (_t,s_) in _G_ remain in _G<sub>f</sub>_, and there is a path from _s_ to _t_ in _G<sub>f</sub>_. If \(t\in S\) and \(s\notin S\), then the arcs (_t,s_)<tbc>

are in \(\partial_{G_f}^+S\), so \(\partial_{G_f}^+S\neq\emptyset\). If \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\), then a path from _s_ to _t_ in _G<sub>f</sub>_ must contain an edge in \(\partial_{G_f}^+S\), so \(\partial_{G_f}^+S\neq\emptyset\). Finally, if \(s,t\in S\) or \(s,t\notin S\), then by the conservation of flow, we have \(|\partial_{G_f}^+S|=|\partial_G^+S|\), and since _G_ is strongly connected by preprocessing, we conclude that \(|\partial_{G_f}^+S|=|\partial_G^+S|\neq 0\).

Our algorithm always finds augmenting paths that avoid the arcs (_t,s_), so while the current flow is not maximum, we may assume that _G<sub>f</sub>_ is strongly connected.

## 2 Balancing Weights

In this section, we construct our balancing weights on the residual graph and describe a data structure to maintain them over the course of the algorithm. The weights assigned to the arcs are determined by a potential function \(\mathbf{y}:V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) on the vertices. For a given potential function **y**, the weight of arc (_u,v_) is

\(w(u,v)=\frac{1}{max\{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u),0\}+1}.\)

In particular, we have \(w(u,v)=\frac{1}{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)+1}\) whenever \(\mathbf{y}(v)\ge\mathbf{y}(u)\), and _w(u,v_)=1 whenever \(\mathbf{y}(v)\le\mathbf{y}(u)\).

The algorithm tries to find a potential function \(\mathbf{y}:V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) such that all cuts are approximately balanced in the two directions: for any set \(S\subseteq V\) , we require that \(\frac{1}{2}w(\partial^-S)\le w(\partial^+S)\le 2w(\partial^-S)\). Actually, we only need to enforce \(\frac{1}{2}w(\partial^-S)\le w(\partial^+S)\) because the other inequality follows by replacing _S_ with _V_\\_S_. If there is a violating set _S_ with \(w(\partial^+S)<\frac{1}{2}w(\partial^-S)\), then the algorithm increases the potential slightly for all vertices in _S_, i.e., sets \(\mathbf{y}(v)\leftarrow\mathbf{y}(v)+\Delta\) for all \(v\in S\), where \(\Delta>0\) is small enough. By a potential function argument, this process must terminate eventually. In particular, a balancing function **y** exists, which is already a non-trivial statement.

To ensure a fast algorithm, we need to find a balancing function **y** quickly, and moreover, dynamically maintain the function upon finding augmenting paths. We interpret the balance of a directed graph as the _minimum ratio cut_ of the underlying _undirected_ graph, and then use the dynamic minimum ratio cut data structure from a recent interior-point method-based flow algorithm \[VDBCK<sup>+</sup>24\].

We first define the minimum ratio cut of an undirected graph, whose input includes a _gradient function_ \(\mathbf{g}:V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) with \(\mathbf{g}\perp\unknown\), i.e., \(\sum_{v\in V}\mathbf{g}(v)=0\).

**Definition 4.** _The_ minimum ratio cut _of a positively weighted, undirected graph with gradient function_ \(\mathbf{g}\perp\unknown\) _is the minimum ratio_ \(\mathbf{g}(S)/w(\partial S)\) _over all_ \(S\subseteq V\) _with_ \(w(\partial S)\neq 0\).

Observe that the requirement \(\mathbf{g}\perp\unknown\) means that **g**(_S_)+**g**(_V_\\_S_)=0 for any \(S\subseteq V\) , so either _S_ or _V_\\_S_ has non-positive ratio. Intuitively, the goal is to maximize |**g**(_S_)| while minimizing \(w(\partial S)\), and then take either _S_ or _V_\\_S_, whichever has non-positive ratio.

We construct our minimum ratio cut instance as follows. Consider the _undirected_ graph with edge weights _w(u,v_) together with the gradient function \(\mathbf{g}:V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) defined as<tbc>

\(\mathbf{g}=\sum_{(u,v)}w(u,v)\cdot(\unknown_u-\unknown_v),\)

i.e., for each arc (_u,v_) in the residual graph, add _w(u,v_) to the tail _u_ and subtract _w(u,v_) from the head _v_. In other words, we "undirect" the residual graph and encode the arc directions through a gradient function. **Lemma 5.** _For any set_ \(S\subseteq V\)_, we have_ \(\mathbf{g}(S)=w(\partial^+S)-w(\partial^-S)\). _Proof._ Any arc \((u,v)\in\partial^+S\) contributes _w(u,v_) to **g**(_S_) since we add _w(u,v_) to the tail \(u\in S\), while the subtraction at the head \(v\notin S\) is not counted in **g**(_S_). Similarly, any arc \((u,v)\in\partial^-S\) contributes -_w(u,v_) to **g**(_S_). All other arcs contribute 0 since either \(u,v\notin S\) in which case there is no contribution, or \(u,v\in S\) in which case the contributions of +_w(u,v_) and -_w(u,v_) cancel out. **Lemma 6.** _If the minimum ratio cut has ratio_ \(\mathbf{g}(S)/w(\partial S)\ge-1/3\)_, then_ \(w(\partial^+S)\ge\frac{1}{2}w(\partial^-S)\) _for all_ \(S\subseteq V\) . _Proof._ It suffices to show that a cut \(S\subseteq V\) with \(w(\partial^+S)<\frac{1}{2}w(\partial^-S)\) implies that \(\mathbf{g}(S)/w(\partial S)<-1/3\). By the previous lemma, we have \(\mathbf{g}(S)=w(\partial^+S)-w(\partial^-S)\). Together with \(w(\partial S)=w(\partial^+S)+w(\partial^-S)\), we obtain \(3\cdot\mathbf{g}(S)+w(\partial S)=3\cdot(w(\partial^+S)-w(\partial^-S))+(w(\partial^+S)+w(\partial^-S))\)
\(=4\cdot w(\partial^+S)-2\cdot w(\partial^-S)\)
\(<2\cdot w(\partial^-S)-2\cdot w(\partial^-S)\)
\(=0,\) or equivalently \(\mathbf{g}(S)/w(\partial S)<-1/3\), as desired. ## 2.1 Dynamic Data Structure To compute and maintain our balancing weights, we use the following data structure defined in \[VDBCK+24\]: **Definition 7** (\(\alpha\)-approximate min-ratio cut data structure, Definition 5.2 of \[VDBCK+24\])**.** _For a weighted undirected graph H_=(_V,E,_**u**) _where_ \(\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^E\) _and_ \(\mathbf{u}(e)\in[1/U,U]^3\) _for_ \(\mathrm{log}U=\tilde{O}(1)\)_, an initial gradient_ \(\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^V\) _where_ \(\mathbf{g}\perp\unknown\) _and_ \(\mathbf{g}(v)\in[-U,U]\)_, an initial potential vector_ \(\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^V\)_, and a detection threshold parameter_ \(\epsilon\)_, an_ \(\alpha\)_-approximate min-ratio cut data structure_ D _implicitly maintains the potential vector_ **y** _and supports the following operations:_ • InsertEdge(_e_),DeleteEdge(_e_)_: inserts/deletes the edge e with weight_ **u**(_e_). • Update\(\mathrm{Gradient}(u,v,\delta)\)_: updates_ \(\mathbf{g}(u)\leftarrow\mathbf{g}(u)+\delta\) _and_ \(\mathbf{g}(v)\leftarrow\mathbf{g}(v)-\delta\). • Potential(_v_)_: returns_ **y**(_v_). 3The only difference is that \[VDBCK+24\] enforces \(\mathbf{u}(e)\in[1,U]\) while we require the weaker \(\mathbf{u}(e)\in[1/U,U]\). However, we can scale all **u**(_e_) and **g**(_v_) by _U_, giving \(\mathbf{u}(e)\in[1,U^2]\) and \(\mathbf{g}(v)\in[-U^2,U^2]\), which preserves all ratios and still satisfies \(\mathrm{log}U^2=\tilde{O}(1)\). We also scale the initial **y** by 1_/U_ and apply their data structure with each \(\eta\) in ToggleCut(\(\eta\)) scaled by 1_/U_, so that the value **u**(_e_)(**y**(_u_)-**y**(_v_)) remains unchanged. Assuming the original constraint \(\mathbf{u}(e)\in[1,U]\) and tracking the scaling by _U_ is cumbersome, so we instead assume the weaker \(\mathbf{u}(e)\in[1/U,U]\) directly.

_The data structure maintains a tuple_ (_g,u_) _where_ \(g\le 0\) _and u\>_0 _such that for some implicit cut_ \(C\subseteq V\) _we have_ **g**(_C_)=_g and_ \(\mathbf{u}(\partial C)\le u\)_, and the (negative) ratio g/u is at most_ \(1/\alpha\) _times the minimum possible over all_ \(C\subseteq V\) .

_The data structure has an additional operation_ \(\mathrm{ToggleCut}(\eta)\) _based on the current tuple_ (_g,u_) _with implicit cut C: given a parameter_ \(0<\eta\le 1/u\)_, the data structure implicitly updates_ \(\mathbf{y}(v)\leftarrow\mathbf{y}(v)+\eta\) _for all_ \(v\in C\)_. Then, the data structure returns some edge set_ \(E'\) _that includes every edge_ \(e=\{u,v\}\in E\) _for which the value_ **u**(_e_)(**y**(_u_)-**y**(_v_)) _has changed by at least an additive_ \(\epsilon\) _since it was inserted/last returned in_ \(E'\).

**Theorem 8** (Theorem 5.4 of \[VDBCK<sup>+</sup>24\])**.** _There is a deterministic_ \(\alpha\)_-approximate min-ratio cut data structure for_ \(\alpha=n^{o(1)}\) _such that every operation is processed in amortized time n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>log_U. Furthermore, the total number of edges returned by the algorithm after t calls to_ \(\mathrm{ToggleCut}(\cdot)\) _is at most_ \(n^{o(1)}\cdot t/\epsilon\).

## 3 Maximum Flow Algorithm

In this section, we present our maximum flow algorithm. We assume access to a dynamic _sparsifier_ data structure which is the focus of the next section (Section 4).

**Definition 9** (Dynamic sparsifier with quality _g_)**.** _For a weighted directed graph H_=(_V,E,_**u**) _where_ \(\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^E\) _and_ \(\mathbf{u}(e)\in[1/U,U]\) _for_ \(\mathrm{log}U=\widetilde{O}(1)\)_, a dynamic sparsifier with quality q supports the following operations:_

• InsertArc(_e),_DeleteArc(_e): inserts/deletes the arc e with weight_ **u**(_e)._<tbc>

• Sparsifier\((\beta)\)_: given_ \(\beta\ge 1\)_, returns a subgraph_ \(\widetilde{H}\subseteq H\) _on at most_ \(q\cdot\beta n\) _arcs such that with high probability, any cut_ \(S\subseteq V\) _with_ \(\mathbf{u}(\partial_H^+S)\ge\frac{1}{\beta}\mathbf{u}(\partial_HS)\) _has at least one sampled out-arc, i.e.,_ \(\partial_H^+S\neq\emptyset\).

**Theorem 10.** _There is a randomized dynamic sparsifier data structure with quality q=n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>log_U such that each call to_ InsertArc(_e),_DeleteArc(_e_) _is processed in amortized time n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>log_U, and each call to_ Sparsifier\((\beta)\) _takes time_ \(O(q\beta n\mathrm{log}U)\).

The algorithm initializes an \(\alpha\)-approximate min-ratio cut data structure (Theorem 8) on the input graph, where **y**=0 and all edges have weight \(w(u,v)=\frac{1}{\mathrm{max}\{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u),0\}+1}=1\). The detection threshold parameter \(\epsilon\) is fixed to \(\epsilon=1/(8\alpha)\). The algorithm only updates arc/edge weights when they pass the detection threshold from the data structure. That is, whenever the data structure returns some edge set \(E'\), the algorithm makes the following updates for each edge \(e\in E'\) with corresponding arc (_u,v_): first, call DeleteEdge(_e_) and UpdateGradient(_u,v,_-**u**(_e_)) to remove the old contribution, and then call InsertEdge(_u,v,w(u,v_)) and UpdateGradient(_u,v,w(u,v_)), where the new weight _w(u,v_) is computed by querying Potential(_u_) and Potential(_v_) to determine **y**(_u_) and **y**(_v_).

The algorithm also initializes a dynamic sparsifier data structure (Theorem 10) with the initial arc weights of 1. Whenever an edge weight is changed in the min-ratio cut data structure, the algorithm propagates the change to the sparsifier data structure.

To find the next augmenting path, the algorithm first computes balancing weights as follows. While the data structure maintains an implicit cut \(C\subseteq V\) with \(g/u\le-1/(3\alpha)\), the algorithm<tbc>

calls ToggleCut(\(\eta\)) with \(\eta=\frac{1}{16\alpha u}\). Otherwise, if \(g/u>-1/(3\alpha)\), then since the data structure is \(\alpha\)-approximate, the minimum ratio cut is at least -1/3. By Lemma 6, we have \(w(\partial^+S)\ge\frac{1}{2}w(\partial^-S)\) for all \(S\subseteq V\) . The actual weights maintained by the data structure are approximations of _w(u,v_), but we show that they are also balanced up to constant factors.

The algorithm calls Sparsifier(\(\beta\)) with \(\beta=9\), obtaining a subgraph on _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> arcs. By the previous balance guarantee, there is an augmenting path from _s_ to _t_ in the sampled graph. The algorithm finds such a path in _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> time and updates both data structures as follows. For each arc _e_=(_v,u_) along the path, the algorithm calls DeleteEdge(_e_)/DeleteArc(_e_) for the corresponding arc/edge (_v,u_), and then InsertEdge(_e_)/InsertArc(_u,v_) with the new weight \(\frac{1}{max\{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u),0\}+1}\) of the flipped arc (_u,v_). The algorithm also calls UpdateGradient accordingly.

## 3.1 Stability

Since edge weights only get updated when they are returned in \(E'\), the data structures only maintain approximations of the true weights. In more detail, for each arc (_u,v_), define the real weight \(w(u,v)=\frac{1}{max\{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u),0\}+1}\) based on the current potential function **y**, and define the approximate weight \(\tilde{w}(u,v)=\mathbf{u}(u,v)\) as the current weight maintained by the data structure, which is the real weight at the last time the corresponding edge (_u,v_) was inserted or returned in \(E'\).

Our algorithm requires that the approximate weights \(\tilde{w}(u,v)\) indeed approximate the real weights. We begin with a stability guarantee on the weight function that is used throughout the analysis.

**Lemma 11** (Stability)**.** _Consider two values_ \(x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}\)_, and define the weights_ \(w_i=\frac{1}{max\{x_i,0\}+1}\) _for_ \(i\in\{1,2\}\)_. For any parameter_ \(0\le\delta<1\)_, if_ \(|x_1-x_2|\le\delta/w_1\)_, then_ \(\frac{1}{1+\delta}w_1\le w_2\le\frac{1}{1-\delta}w_1\).

_Proof._ We bound

\(w_2=\frac{1}{max\{x_2,0\}+1}\ge\frac{1}{max\{x_1+\delta/w_1,0\}+1}\ge\frac{1}{max\{x_1,0\}+1+\delta/w_1}=\frac{1}{1/w_1+\delta/w_1}=\frac{w_1}{1+\delta}\)

and

\(w_2=\frac{1}{max\{x_2,0\}+1}\le\frac{1}{max\{x_1-\delta/w_1,0\}+1}\le\frac{1}{max\{x_1,0\}+1-\delta/w_1}=\frac{1}{1/w_1-\delta/w_1}=\frac{w_1}{1-\delta}\)

as desired.

**Lemma 12** (Approximation of weights)**.** _For any arc_ (_u,v), we have_ \(\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}\tilde{w}(u,v)\le w(u,v)\le\frac{1}{1-\epsilon}\tilde{w}(u,v)\).

_Proof._ Let \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\) be the potential function when the edge (_u,v_) was last inserted or returned in \(E'\). In particular, \(\tilde{w}(u,v)=\frac{1}{max\{\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(v)-\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(u),0\}+1}\). By the guarantee of the data structure, we have

\(\tilde{w}(u,v)\cdot|(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(u)-\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(v))-(\mathbf{y}(u)-\mathbf{y}(v))|<\epsilon\Longleftrightarrow|(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(u)-\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(v))-(\mathbf{y}(u)-\mathbf{y}(v))|<\epsilon/\tilde{w}(u,v).\)

Applying Lemma 11 with \(x_1=\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(u)-\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(v)\) and _x_<sub>2</sub>=**y**(_u_)-**y**(_v_) and \(\delta=\epsilon\) finishes the proof.

Finally, we show that if the algorithm stops calling ToggleCut(\(\eta\)), at which point \(g/u>-1/(3\alpha)\), then the (approximate) edge weights maintained by the data structure are balanced. In particular, Sparsifier(\(\beta\)) with \(\beta=9\) returns a subgraph containing an augmenting path from _s_ to _t_ with high probability.

**Lemma 13.** _If_ \(g/u>-1/(3\alpha)\)_, then_ \(\tilde{w}(\partial^+S)\ge\frac{1}{9}\tilde{w}(\partial S)\) _for all_ \(S\subseteq V\) .

_Proof._ By Lemma 6, we have \(w(\partial^+S)\ge\frac{1}{2}w(\partial^-S)\) for all \(S\subseteq V\) . Together with Lemma 12, we have \(2\tilde{w}(\partial^+S)\ge w(\partial^+S)\ge\frac{1}{2}w(\partial^-S)\ge\frac{1}{4}\tilde{w}(\partial^-S)\), so \(\tilde{w}(\partial^+S)\ge\frac{1}{8}\tilde{w}(\partial^-S)\), or equivalently \(\tilde{w}(\partial^+S)\ge\frac{1}{9}\tilde{w}(\partial S)\).

## 3.2 Energy Bounds

To bound the running time, we need to track the number of calls to ToggleCut. Let _M=n_<sup>_O_(1)</sup> be large enough, and define the _energy_ of arc (_u,v_) as<tbc>

\(\mathcal{E}(u,v)=\int_{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)}^M\frac{1}{max\{x,0\}+1}dx.\)

<tbc>Observe that

\(\mathcal{E}(u,v)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
ln(M+1)-ln(\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)+1) & \text{if}\mathbf{y}(v)\ge\mathbf{y}(u), \\
ln(M+1)+\mathbf{y}(u)-\mathbf{y}(v) & \text{if}\mathbf{y}(v)\le\mathbf{y}(u).
\end{array}\right.\)

The following lemma shows that each call to ToggleCut decreases the total energy by an additive 1_/n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>.

**Lemma 14** (Energy decrease)**.** _On each call to_ ToggleCut_, the total energy decreases by at least_ \(\Omega(1/\alpha^3)\).

_Proof._ On each call to ToggleCut\((\eta)\), the implicit cut _C_ satisfies \(g/u\le-1/(3\alpha)\), where **g**(_C_)=_g\<_0 and \(\mathbf{u}(\partial C)\le u\). We also have \(\mathbf{u}(\partial C)\ge u/\alpha\) since otherwise, if \(\mathbf{u}(\partial C)<u/\alpha\), then the ratio \(\mathbf{g}(C)/\mathbf{u}(\partial C)\) would be less than \(\mathbf{g}(C)/(u/\alpha)=\alpha\cdot g/u\), contradicting the fact that _g/u_ is at most \(1/\alpha\) times the min-ratio cut.

We now analyze the contribution of ToggleCut\((\eta)\) to the total energy. Let _w_ and **y** be the weight and potential function immediately before ToggleCut\((\eta)\). For each arc \((u,v)\in\partial^+C\), the value of **y**(_u_) is increased by \(\eta\), so the energy E(_u,v_) increases by<tbc>

\(\int_{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)-\eta}^{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)}\frac{1}{max\{x,0\}+1}dx.\)

<tbc>Similarly, for each arc \((u,v)\in\partial^-C\), the value of **y**(_v_) is increased by \(\eta\), so the energy E(_u,v_) decreases by<tbc>

\(\int_{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)}^{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)+\eta}\frac{1}{max\{x,0\}+1}dx.\)

<tbc>By the approximation of weights (Lemma 12), we have \(w(u,v)\le 2\tilde{w}(u,v)\), so for any arc \((u,v)\in\partial C\), we have \(u\ge\mathbf{u}(\partial C)\ge\tilde{w}(u,v)\ge\frac{1}{2}w(u,v)\). Since \(\eta=\frac{1}{16\alpha u}\le\frac{1}{8\alpha\cdot w(u,v)}\), by the stability guarantee (Lemma 11) with \(\delta=\frac{1}{8\alpha}\), we have<tbc>

\(\frac{1}{1+1/(8\alpha)}w(u,v)\le\frac{1}{max\{x,0\}+1}\le\frac{1}{1-1/(8\alpha)}w(u,v)\text{for all}x\in[\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)-\eta,\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)+\eta].\)

In particular, the energy increase of each arc \((u,v)\in\partial^+C\) is at most \(\eta\cdot\frac{1}{1-1/(8\alpha)}\cdot w(u,v)\), and the energy decrease from each arc \((u,v)\in\partial^-C\) is at least \(\eta\cdot\frac{1}{1+1/(8\alpha)}\cdot w(u,v)\). Summed over all such arcs, the net change in energy is at most \(\eta\cdot\frac{1}{1-1/(8\alpha)}\cdot w(\partial^+C)-\eta\cdot\frac{1}{1+1/(8\alpha)}\cdot w(\partial^-C).\) Recall that \(\mathbf{g}(C)/\mathbf{u}(\partial C)\le g/u\le-1/(3\alpha)\) and \(\mathbf{g}(C)=\tilde{w}(\partial^+C)-\tilde{w}(\partial^-C)\) and \(\mathbf{u}(\partial C)=\tilde{w}(\partial^+C)+\tilde{w}(\partial^-C)\). We have \(3\alpha\cdot\mathbf{g}(C)+\mathbf{u}(\partial C)\le 0\Longleftrightarrow(3\alpha+1)\cdot\tilde{w}(\partial^+C)-(3\alpha-1)\cdot\tilde{w}(\partial^-C)\le 0\)
\(\Longleftrightarrow\tilde{w}(\partial^+C)\le\frac{3\alpha-1}{3\alpha+1}\cdot\tilde{w}(\partial^-C).\) Together with the approximation of weights (Lemma 12), we have \(w(\partial^+C)\le\frac{1}{1-\epsilon}\cdot\tilde{w}(\partial^+C)\le\frac{1}{1-\epsilon}\cdot\frac{3\alpha-1}{3\alpha+1}\cdot\tilde{w}(\partial^-C)\le\frac{1}{1-\epsilon}\cdot\frac{3\alpha-1}{3\alpha+1}\cdot(1+\epsilon)\cdot w(\partial^-C).\) Since \(\epsilon=1/(8\alpha)\), it follows that the net change in energy is at most \(\eta\cdot\frac{1}{1-1/(8\alpha)}\cdot w(\partial^+C)-\eta\cdot\frac{1}{1+1/(8\alpha)}\cdot w(\partial^-C)\)
\(\le\eta\cdot\frac{1}{1-1/(8\alpha)}\cdot\frac{1+1/(8\alpha)}{1-1/(8\alpha)}\cdot\frac{3\alpha-1}{3\alpha+1}\cdot w(\partial^-C)-\eta\cdot\frac{1}{1+1/(8\alpha)}\cdot w(\partial^-C)\)
\(\le\eta\cdot-\Omega\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)\cdot w(\partial^-C)\)
\(\le\eta\cdot-\Omega\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)\cdot\tilde{w}(\partial^-C).\) Recall that \(\mathbf{u}(\partial C)\ge u/\alpha\), which means that \(\eta=\frac{1}{16\alpha u}\ge\frac{1}{16\alpha^2\mathbf{u}(\partial C)}\). Also, since **g**(_C)\<_0, we have \(\tilde{w}(\partial^-C)\ge\frac{1}{2}\tilde{w}(\partial C)=\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u}(\partial C)\). We conclude that the net change in energy is at most \(\frac{1}{16\alpha^2\mathbf{u}(\partial C)}\cdot-\Omega\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)\cdot\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u}(\partial C)=-\Omega\left(\frac{1}{\alpha^3}\right),\) as desired. Next, suppose that the algorithm finds an augmenting path from _s_ to _t_. The following lemma bounds the total increase in energy from flipping the arcs along the augmenting path. **Lemma 15** (Energy increase)**.** _Assume that all vertex potentials are within an additive M of each other, i.e.,_ \(|\mathbf{y}(u)-\mathbf{y}(v)|\le M\) _for all_ \(u,v\in V\) _. Suppose the algorithm flips all arcs along a (simple) path from s to t. The total energy increases by at most_ **y**(_t_)-**y**(_s_)+(_n_-1)ln(_M_+1). _Proof._ Recall that \(\mathcal{E}(u,v)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } ln(M+1)-ln(\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)+1) & \text{if}\mathbf{y}(v)\ge\mathbf{y}(u), \\ ln(M+1)+\mathbf{y}(u)-\mathbf{y}(v) & \text{if}\mathbf{y}(v)\le\mathbf{y}(u). \end{array}\right.\)

Consider the energy difference from flipping an individual arc (_u,v_). If \(\mathbf{y}(v)\ge\mathbf{y}(u)\), then the original energy is ln(_M_+1)-ln(**y**(_v_)-**y**(_u_)+1) and the new energy is ln(_M_+1)+**y**(_v_)-**y**(_u_), so the net change in energy is \(\big(ln(M+1)+\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)\big)-\big(ln(M+1)-ln(\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)+1)\big)\)
\(=\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)+ln(\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)+1)\)
\(\le\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)+ln(M+1),\) where we use the assumption that \(\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)\le M\). Similarly, if \(\mathbf{y}(v)\le\mathbf{y}(u)\), then the original energy is ln(_M_+1)+**y**(_u_)-**y**(_v_) and the new energy is ln(_M_+1)-ln(**y**(_u_)-**y**(_v_)+1), so the net change in energy is \(\big(ln(M+1)-ln(\mathbf{y}(u)-\mathbf{y}(v)+1)\big)-\big(ln(M+1)+\mathbf{y}(u)-\mathbf{y}(v)\big)\)
\(=\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)-ln(\mathbf{y}(u)-\mathbf{y}(v)+1)\)
\(\le\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u).\) In both cases, the net change in energy is at most **y**(_v_)-**y**(_u_)+ln(_M_+1). Summed over all arcs (_u,v_) on the path, the **y**(_v_)-**y**(_u_) terms telescope to **y**(_t_)-**y**(_s_), and the ln(_M_+1) terms sum to at most (_n_-1)ln(_M_+1). ## 3.3 Running Time Outside of the calls to ToggleCut, the algorithm spends _n_1+_o_(1) time on each augmenting path: the algorithm computes a sparsifier, finds an augmenting path, flips the path, and updates the data structures. To bound the number of calls to ToggleCut, it suffices to bound the total energy increase over the course of the algorithm, since the total energy starts at _m_ln(_M_+1) and decreases by \(\Omega(\alpha^3)=1/n^{o(1)}\) on each call to ToggleCut (Lemma 14). Let E be the current total energy. By Lemma 15, the energy increase is at most **y**(_t_)-**y**(_s_)+(_n_-1)ln(_M_+1) after flipping the next augmenting path. If \(\mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(s)\ge 0\), then we bound **y**(_t_)-**y**(_s_) as follows. Each of the arcs (_t,s_) added during preprocessing has energy \(ln(M+1)+\mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(s)\ge\mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(s)\). There are \(\Omega(m)\) such arcs, so their total energy \(\Omega(m)\cdot(\mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(s))\) is at most E. We conclude that \(\mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(s)\le O(\mathcal{E}/m)\), and the total energy after flipping the augmenting path is at most \((1+O(1/m))\cdot\mathcal{E}+(n-1)ln(M+1)\). The total number of augmenting paths is \(F\le m\), so the total energy increase is at most \((1+O(1/m))^F\cdot(mln(M+1)+F(n-1)ln(M+1))\le O((m+nF)ln(M+1))\). At this point, we can also justify the assumption \(max_{u,v}|\mathbf{y}(u)-\mathbf{y}(v)|\le M\) from Lemma 15 for _M=n__O_(1) as long as the residual graph is strongly connected. For the sake of argument, re-define _M_ as the largest value of max_u,v_|**y**(_u_)-**y**(_v_)| over the course of the algorithm, and suppose for contradiction that _M_ is too large. Consider the moment of the algorithm at which **y**(_u_)-**y**(_v_)=_M_ for some \(u,v\in V\) . Consider a path from _u_ to _v_ of at most _n_-1 arcs in the current residual graph. There is an arc \((u',v')\) on the path with \(\mathbf{y}(u')-\mathbf{y}(v')\ge M/(n-1)\), which has energy \(ln(M+1)+\mathbf{y}(u')-\mathbf{y}(v')\ge M/(n-1)\). In particular, the total energy is at least _M/(n_-1). However, by the previous energy bound, the total energy at this point is at most _O_((_m+nF_)ln(_M_+1)). For large enough _M=n__O_(1), we obtain a contradiction. We conclude that the algorithm has total running time \((m+nF)\cdot n^{o(1)}\) while the residual graph is strongly connected. When the flow is maximum, the residual graph _Gf_ is no longer strongly connected, and the algorithm may have undefined behavior. However, we can impose a running

time limit of \((m+n|f|)\cdot n^{o(1)}\) where |_f_| is the current flow value, and terminate the algorithm if the limit is exceeded. This completes the proof of our main result (Theorem 1).

To obtain Corollary 2, we use the fact that \(\sqrt{n}\) rounds of Dinic’s blocking flow algorithm \[Din70\] reduces the maximum flow of the residual graph to at most \(m/\sqrt{n}\) \[Kar73, ET75\]. Computing the blocking flows takes time \(O(m\sqrt{n})\), and applying Theorem 1 with \(F\le m/\sqrt{n}\) on the residual graph takes time _mn_<sup>1/2+_o_(1)</sup>.

## 4 Dynamic Sparsification

In this section, we present our dynamic sparsifier data structure to establish Theorem 10, restated below together with the definition.

**Definition 9** (Dynamic sparsifier with quality _q_)**.** _For a weighted directed graph H_=(_V,E,_**u**) _where_ \(\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^E\) _and_ \(\mathbf{u}(e)\in[1/U,U]\) _for_ \(\mathrm{log}U=\widetilde{O}(1)\)_, a dynamic sparsifier with quality q supports the following operations:_

• InsertArc(_e),_DeleteArc(_e): inserts/deletes the arc e with weight_ **u**(_e)._<tbc>

• Sparsifier\((\beta)\)_: given_ \(\beta\ge 1\)_, returns a subgraph_ \(\widetilde{H}\subseteq H\) _on at most_ \(q\cdot\beta n\) _arcs such that with high probability, any cut_ \(S\subseteq V\) _with_ \(\mathbf{u}(\partial_H^+S)\ge\frac{1}{\beta}\mathbf{u}(\partial_HS)\) _has at least one sampled out-arc, i.e.,_ \(\partial_\widetilde{H}^+S\neq\emptyset\).

**Theorem 10.** _There is a randomized dynamic sparsifier data structure with quality q=n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>log_U such that each call to_ InsertArc(_e),_DeleteArc(_e_) _is processed in amortized time n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>log_U, and each call to_ Sparsifier\((\beta)\) _takes time_ \(O(q\beta n\mathrm{log}U)\).

### 4.1 Reduction to Unweighted Graphs

The dynamic algorithm first reduces to the case of unweighted graphs by bucketing the arcs and running an unweighted dynamic sparsifier with quality _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> on each bucket. More precisely, for each integer _i_, let \(H_i\subseteq H\) be the subgraph of all arcs with weight in the range \[2_<sup>i</sup>,_2<sup>_i_+1</sup>). Since \(\mathbf{u}(e)\in[1/U,U]\), there are only _O_(log_U_) non-empty subgraphs _H<sub>i</sub>_. For each _H<sub>i</sub>_, treated as a dynamic _unweighted_ graph, initialize a dynamic sparsifier data structure where all arcs have weight 1. Finally, on each query to Sparsifier\((\beta)\), the algorithm calls Sparsifier\((2\beta)\) on the data structure for each _H<sub>i</sub>_, obtaining a subgraph \(\widetilde{H}_i\subseteq H_i\). The algorithm outputs the union of the subgraphs \(\widetilde{H}_i\) as the final sparsifier \(\widetilde{H}\), which has \(q\cdot\beta n\cdot O(\mathrm{log}U)\) arcs.

To prove correctness of this reduction, consider a cut \(S\subseteq V\) with \(\mathbf{u}(\partial_H^+S)\ge\frac{1}{\beta}\mathbf{u}(\partial_HS)\), rewritten as \(\beta\cdot\mathbf{u}(\partial_H^+S)-\mathbf{u}(\partial_HS)\ge 0\). By our bucketing scheme, we can bound \(\mathbf{u}(\partial_H^+S)\) and \(\mathbf{u}(\partial_HS)\) by<tbc>

\(\mathbf{u}(\partial_H^+S)\le\sum_i2^{i+1}\cdot|\partial_{H_i}^+S|\text{and}\mathbf{u}(\partial_HS)\ge\sum_i2^i\cdot|\partial_{H_i}S|,\)

<tbc>so

\(\sum_i2^i\cdot(2\beta\cdot|\partial_{H_i}^+S|-|\partial_{H_i}S|)=\beta\cdot\sum_i2^{i+1}\cdot|\partial_{H_i}^+S|-\sum_i2^i\cdot|\partial_{H_i}S|\ge\beta\cdot\mathbf{u}(\partial_H^+S)-\mathbf{u}(\partial_HS)\ge 0.\)

In particular, there exists an _i_ with \(2\beta\cdot|\partial_{H_i}^+S|-|\partial_{H_i}S|\ge 0\), or equivalently \(|\partial_{H_i}^+S|\ge\frac{1}{2\beta}|\partial_{H_i}S|\). Assuming that the guarantee of Sparsifier\((2\beta)\) on _H<sub>i</sub>_ holds, we conclude that \(\partial_{\widetilde{H}_i}^+S\neq\emptyset\) as well as \(\partial_\widetilde{H}^+S\neq\emptyset\), completing the reduction.

## 4.2 Dynamic Unweighted Sparsifier

For the dynamic unweighted sparsifier, the algorithm maintains a sequence of explicit _expander decompositions_ of the underlying undirected graph. We begin with some expander decomposition preliminaries on unweighted, undirected graphs. For a subset of vertices \(S\subseteq V\) , let \(\mathbf{vol}(S)=\sum_{v\in S}deg(v)\) denote the sum of vertex degrees in _S_. For a partition P={_V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>k</sub>_} of _V_ into clusters, let \(\partial\mathcal{P}=\cup_{i=1}^k\partial V_i\) denote the edges whose endpoints belong to different clusters.

**Definition 16** (\(\phi\)-expander)**.** _An undirected graph is a_ \(\phi\)-expander _if_ \(|\partial S|\ge\phi\cdot min\{\mathbf{vol}(S)\), **vol**(_V_\\_S_)} _for all_ \(S\subseteq V\) .

**Definition 17** (\(\phi\)-expander decomposition with slack _s_)**.** _A_ \(\phi\)_-expander decomposition of an undirected graph G with slack_ \(s\ge 1\) _is a partition_ P={_V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>k</sub>_} _of V into clusters such that_

1. \(|\partial\mathcal{P}|\le\tilde{O}(\phi m)\)_, and_<tbc>

_2._ _Each induced subgraph G_\[_V<sub>i</sub>_\] _is a_ \((\phi/s)\)_-expander._

We are interested in a dynamic expander decomposition algorithm with low _recourse_ with respect to the set \(\partial\mathcal{P}\). We say that the algorithm has amortized recourse \(\rho\) if for all \(k\ge 1\), the set \(\partial\mathcal{P}\) changes by at most \(\rho\cdot k\) edges after _k_ edge updates to the graph.

**Theorem 18** (Theorem 7.2 of \[GRST21\])**.** _Let_ \(0<\phi<1\) _be a parameter. There is a randomized algorithm that, given an unweighted graph G undergoing edge insertions and deletions, maintains an explicit_ \(\phi\)_-expander decomposition with slack_ \(s=2^{-O(log^{1/2}n)}\) _together with the explicit set of edges_ \(\partial\mathcal{P}\)_. The algorithm has update time_ \(2^{O(\sqrt{logn})}/\phi^2\) _and amortized recourse_ \(2^{O(\sqrt{logn})}\) _with respect to_ \(\partial\mathcal{P}\)_. The algorithm succeeds with high probability against an adaptive adversary._

We now describe the dynamic sparsification algorithm. Given the graph _H_, the algorithm first adds between _m/n_ and 2_m/n_ self-loops to each vertex in _H_. This initial pre-processing has amortized recourse _O_(1) since it takes \(\Omega(m)\) edge updates before the value of _m/n_ changes by a constant factor, at which point _O(m_) time is spent updating the self-loops. After the addition of self- loops, the graph still has _O(m_) edges. The algorithm maintains a dynamic expander decomposition (Theorem 18) with parameter \(\phi=2^{-log^{3/4}n}\) on the graph with self-loops. On the subgraph of _H_ consisting of the edges \(\partial\mathcal{P}\), the algorithm _recursively_ performs the same procedure, starting with adding \(|\partial\mathcal{P}|/n\) self-loops to each vertex. Since \(|\partial\mathcal{P}|\) is a factor \(2^{\Omega(log^{3/4}n)}\) smaller, the recursion depth is _t=O_(log<sup>1/4</sup>_n_). Each level of recursion has amortized recourse \(2^{O(\sqrt{logn})}\), so the overall recourse (and update time) is 2<sup>_O_(log<sup>3/4</sup>_n_)</sup>.

Given the explicitly maintained expander decompositions, we now implement the procedure \(\text{Sparsifier}(\beta)\). On recursion level \(i\ge 0\), let \(G_i\subseteq H\) be the initial subgraph at level \(i\ge 0\) of recursion (before the addition of self-loops), and let _m<sub>i</sub>_ be the number of edges in _G<sub>i</sub>_. Let P_<sub>i</sub>_ be the expander decomposition at this level, and let \(H_i=G_i\backslash\partial\mathcal{P}_i\) be the subgraph of edges with both endpoints in the same cluster. By construction, the input graph _H_ is the disjoint union of the subgraphs _H<sub>i</sub>_. The algorithm independently samples each edge in _H<sub>i</sub>_ with probability \(\frac{q\beta}{2t}\cdot\frac{n}{m_i}\), and outputs the sparsifier \(\widetilde{H}\) as the union of all sampled edges (over all _i_).

For the running time, observe that for each _i_, the random sampling in _H<sub>i</sub>_ can be done in time proportional to the number of samples: first determine the number of samples _s_, which can be sampled from a binomial distribution, and then randomly sample _s_ edges from the edges in _H<sub>i</sub>_.<tbc>

The expected number of samples in _H<sub>i</sub>_ is at most \(\frac{q\beta}{2t}\cdot n\), so the sparsifier \(\widetilde{H}\) has expected size at most \(q\beta n/2\). A simple concentration bound shows that the size is at most \(q\beta n\) with high probability, so the running time is also \(O(q\beta n)\) with high probability.

It remains to establish the sparsifier guarantee. Consider a cut \(S\subseteq V\) with \(|\partial_H^+S|\ge\frac{1}{\beta}|\partial_HS|\), rewritten as \(\beta\cdot|\partial_H^+S|-|\partial_HS|\ge 0\). Since _H_ is the disjoint union of subgraphs _H<sub>i</sub>_, we can write \(|\partial_H^+S|=\sum_i|\partial_{H_i}^+S|\) and similarly for \(\partial_HS\). In particular,

\(\sum_i(\beta\cdot|\partial_{H_i}^+S|-|\partial_{H_i}S|)=\beta\cdot\sum_i|\partial_{H_i}^+S|-\sum_i|\partial_{H_i}S|=\beta\cdot|\partial_H^+S|-|\partial_HS|\ge 0,\)

so for some _i_, we have \(\beta\cdot|\partial_{H_i}^+S|-|\partial_{H_i}S|\ge 0\). We can further write _H<sub>i</sub>_ as the disjoint union of \(\phi\)-expanders from the decomposition P_<sub>i</sub>_, and by a similar argument, there is a \(\phi\)-expander \(X\subseteq H_i\) supported on \(U\subseteq V\) with \(\beta\cdot|\partial_X^+(S\cap U)|-|\partial_X(S\cap U)|\ge 0\).

Our goal is to show that for a fixed \(\phi\)-expander \(X\subseteq H_i\) supported on \(U\subseteq V\) , with high probability, any cut \(R\subseteq U\) with \(\beta\cdot|\partial_X^+R|-|\partial_XR|\ge 0\) has at least one sampled out-arc in _X_. Taking a union bound over all expanders _X_ (over all levels of recursion) then handles all cuts \(S\subseteq V\) in the sparsifier guarantee, completing the proof.

Consider a \(\phi\)-expander \(X\subseteq H_i\) supported on \(U\subseteq V\) . We establish a "cut counting" style union bound by grouping the cuts \(R\subseteq U\) with \(\beta\cdot|\partial_X^+R|-|\partial_XR|\ge 0\) by the value min{|_R|,|U_\\_R_|}. For each integer \(k\ge 1\), there are at most \(2\cdot|U|^k\) many cuts \(R\subseteq U\) with min{|_R|,|U_\\_R_|}=_k_. By the \(\phi\)-expander guarantee, each such cut satisfies \(|\partial_XR|\ge\phi\cdot min\{\mathbf{vol}_X(R),\mathbf{vol}_X(U\backslash R)\}\). Since at least _m<sub>i</sub>/n_ self-loops were added to each vertex before the expander decomposition, we have \(min\{\mathbf{vol}_X(R),\mathbf{vol}_X(U\backslash R)\}\ge m_i/n\cdot min\{|R|,|U\backslash R|\}=km_i/n\). In particular, if \(\beta\cdot|\partial_X^+R|-|\partial_XR|\ge 0\), then \(|\partial_X^+R|\ge\frac{1}{\beta}|\partial_XR|\ge\frac{k\phi}{\beta}\cdot\frac{m_i}{n}\) . Each edge in _X_ is sampled with probability \(\frac{q\beta}{2t}\cdot\frac{n}{m_i}\), so the probability of sampling no edge in \(\partial_X^+R\) is

\(\left(1-\frac{q\beta}{2t}\cdot\frac{n}{m_i}\right)^{|\partial_X^+R|}\le exp\left(-\frac{q\beta}{2t}\cdot\frac{n}{m_i}\cdot|\partial_X^+R|\right)\le exp\left(-\frac{q\beta}{2t}\cdot\frac{n}{m_i}\cdot\frac{k\phi}{\beta}\cdot\frac{m_i}{n}\right)=exp\left(-\frac{kq\phi}{2t}\right).\)

Setting \(q=2ct/\phi\cdot lnn\) for an arbitrary constant _c\>_0, this probability is at most exp(-_ck_ln_n_)=_n_<sup>-_ck_</sup>. Taking a union bound over all cuts \(R\subseteq U\) with min{|_R|,|U_\\_R_|}=_k_, the probability of failure is at most \(2\cdot|U|^k\cdot n^{-ck}\le 2n^{-(c-1)k}\) for this value of _k_. Finally, taking a union bound over all \(k\ge 1\), the overall probability of failure is at most \(\sum_{k\ge 1}2n^{-(c-1)k}\le O(n^{-(c-1)})\), as desired.

## 5 Conclusion

We conclude with some future directions. The first question is whether our weight function \(w(u,v)=\frac{1}{max\{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u),0\}+1}\) is the "right" function. A more natural function is \(\frac{1}{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)+1}\), which induces a "barrier" that enforces \(\mathbf{y}(v)\ge\mathbf{y}(u)-1\) in the same way the push-relabel algorithm requires \(d(v)\ge d(u)-1\) on arcs (_u,v_) in the residual graph \[GT88\]. However, our algorithm may flip an "upward" arc (_v,u_) with \(\mathbf{y}(v)\checkmark\mathbf{y}(u)-1\), causing the new weight \(\frac{1}{\mathbf{y}(v)-\mathbf{y}(u)+1}\) to be undefined. On the other hand, the push-relabel algorithm never sends flow along upward arcs, so perhaps the algorithm should only flip downward arcs. We leave as an open question whether our algorithm can be adapted to behave like a "continuous" push-relabel algorithm.

Another question is whether the balancing weights technique can be applied to other directed graph problems. Balanced directed graphs behave similarly to undirected graphs, so the method<tbc>

can be viewed as a way to apply the powerful techniques for undirected graphs to the more difficult setting of directed graphs. Indeed, the recent interior point method-based flow algorithms [CKL<sup>+</sup>25, VDBCK<sup>+</sup>24] all adopt this strategy to great success: each iteration reduces to a problem on an undirected graph, which is solved quickly by dynamic data structures.

Finally, one limit to the current balancing weights approach is the requirement that the graph is strongly connected. We leave as an open question whether the technique can be extended to general directed graphs. One difficulty in handling cuts with no arcs in one direction is that the arcs in the other direction may have their weights approaching 0, which means that **y**(_v_)-**y**(_u_) becomes arbitrarily large. One possible approach is to employ a "softer" weight function to control the potential differences as the weights tend to 0.
